headings.title: Introduction to Solutions and Solutes
headings.content: A solution is a homogeneous mixture composed of two or more substances. In any solution, the substance present in the smaller amount is called the **solute**, while the substance present in the greater amount is the **solvent**. In clinical midwifery, water acts as the primary universal solvent, dissolving various chemical substances to form vital body fluids such as blood plasma, interstitial fluid, and intracellular fluid. When a solid, liquid, or gas dissolves, its particles disperse evenly throughout the solvent at the molecular or ionic level. Understanding how different solutes behave when dissolved forms the foundation of fluid and electrolyte balance management in pregnant and laboring women.

headings.title: Understanding Electrolytes
headings.content: Electrolytes are substances that release ions when dissolved in water, producing a solution that can conduct an electrical current. These particles carry either a positive charge (**cations**) or a negative charge (**anions**). Common clinical examples include sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride. In the human body, these charged particles are indispensable for generating action potentials in nerves and muscle fibers, maintaining proper hydration, and regulating acid-base balance. When salts dissolve, their ionic bonds dissociate completely, freeing the individual ions to move independently through the fluid.

headings.title: Characteristics of Non-Electrolytes
headings.content: Non-electrolytes are substances that dissolve in water as intact, neutral molecules rather than breaking down into ions. Because they do not form free charges in solution, their aqueous solutions cannot conduct electricity. Typical examples include glucose, urea, and various alcohols. When sucrose dissolves in water, the individual sugar molecules separate from one another, but every single molecule remains entirely neutral and intact. Midwives encounter non-electrolytes frequently when administering intravenous dextrose solutions to patients requiring caloric support without ionic disturbance.

headings.title: Comparing Electrical Conductivity
headings.content:
The fundamental difference between electrolytes and non-electrolytes lies in their behavior toward electric current. Strong electrolytes dissociate completely, allowing a high current to pass and illuminating a conductivity test bulb brightly. Weak electrolytes dissociate only partially, resulting in a dim light. Non-electrolytes do not dissociate into ions at all, resulting in no current flow and no light emission.

| Solute Type | Degree of Dissociation | Conductivity in Solution |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Strong Electrolyte | High / Complete | High |
| Weak Electrolyte | Low / Partial | Low |
| Non-Electrolyte | None (Intact molecules) | None (Zero) |

headings.title: Clinical Significance in Midwifery Practice
headings.content: Electrolytes play critical roles in regulating fluid shifts, maintaining blood pressure, and enabling muscular contractions throughout the body. During labor, precise balance of sodium, potassium, and calcium is vital for effective uterine myometrial contractions and maternal cardiac stability. Severe imbalances can lead to complications such as pre-eclamptic seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, or severe muscle cramps. Midwives must monitor hydration and electrolyte status closely, particularly when administering intravenous fluids or managing women experiencing prolonged vomiting during early pregnancy.
